newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian sub-continent prices seen falling.
newsitem.headline: Indian sub-continent prices seen falling.

text.p: Prices of gold in India and Pakistan are likely to fall this week with imported metal costs rising in the Indian sub-continent, dealers said on Monday.
Dealers said vigilance in India's major cities, especially Bombay, the country's main bullion trading centre, affected the movement of gold ahead of Sunday, the Republic Day.
They said gold imports into Bombay had fallen last week due to a strict security vigil at key places such as the city's international airport and bullion market.
In Bombay standard gold (24 carats) rose 30 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,930 in the week to Monday because of the reduced supplies.
"Gold prices bounced back on fresh seasonal buying, aided by poor supplies and a shortage of ready stock," said leading jeweller Babubhai Jain.
Jain said gold could lose some of its previous week's gains in the next few days on fresh imports.
"But the overall market trend still depends on price movements in the world market," said dealer Mahavir Shah.
"Any fall in gold prices will attract buying during the six-month-long wedding season which lasts up to May," Shah said.
In Pakistan's main commercial city of Karachi, gold prices are expected to fall this week following the end of monopoly imports by a gold trading house.
Dealers said supplies are expected to improve from this week with the government allowing two more companies to import gold, ending a two-year monopoly enjoyed by ARY Traders.
Standard gold fell 120 rupees per 10 grammes to a four-month low of 4,962 rupees in the week to Sunday.
One dealer said lower prices also reflected a steep fall in bullion markets abroad, where gold fell below $350 an ounce.

The Pakistan government has authorised Karachi-based M.R. Rahim and Lahore-based Mohammad Al-Ramzan to import gold and silver, subject to a duty of $1.40 per tola (11.664 grammes) for gold and $2 per kg for silver.
Dealers said the possible competition among the authorised importers may push gold prices below 4,500 rupees per 10 grammes.

In the Gulf trading hub of Dubai, the centre for gold exports into India and Pakistan, the demand for bullion and jewellery had not yet picked up in the closing weeks of the Islamic fasting month of Ramadan, dealers said on Sunday.
The Eid al-Fitr holiday marking the end of Ramadan is due in the Gulf around February 10 and is traditionally an auspicious time for buying precious metal in the oil region.
Demand from the main Indian import market was steady because of continued wedding demand and relaxed import rules at the start of the 1997 calendar year.
"The margins into India are still reasonable and the wedding season is there. But it's nothing spectacular," a trader said.
